messages.subject: Simulating datasets with a rw2 smoother for a covariate
messages.subject_clean: Simulating datasets with a rw2 smoother for a covariate
messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,

Quick question here, I have a Bernoulli GAM spatial model that i want to validate. Previously I have done this by simulating 1000 datasets and comparing the number of zeros, or the dispersion statistic, according to the methods outlined in Zuur et al., 2017.

I added a rw2 smoother to one of my variables which has caused a hiccup, in that i need to adjust the covariate matrix to account for the extra hyperparameters (I'm getting the usual: "Error in Xmat %*% Betas : non-conformable arguments".

So, the question is, how do i write the covariate in question to include the rw2?

Say my covariate matrix is:

Covariates <- data.frame(
  Intercept   = rep(1, N),
  bath.std      = Skate$bath.std,
  current.std      = Skate$current.std,
  dcoast.std      = Skate$dcoast.std,
  sal.std      = Skate$sal.std,
  mud.std      = Skate$mud.std,
  gravel.std  = Skate$gravel.std
)

bath.std is the covariate I want to smooth with rw2, any advice would be very much appreciated.

messages.subject: Help fixing cox model with patterns in martingale residuals and broad credible intervals
messages.subject_clean: Help fixing cox model with patterns in martingale residuals and broad credible intervals
messages.body_plain:
Dear everyone,

I am trying to fit a cox model with inla but struggle with my model residuals and the credible intervals. I am only able to show the model diagnostic plots but hope you can share your insights if there is anything to be done to fix the errors in the residuals and make the estimates a pit more precise.

I have two         successive experiments including 4 experimental groups with a relatively small sample size and one control group which I fit with

inla(inla.surv(day_study_s, status) ~ 1 + group + mean_vol,
                    data = df, family = "coxph", control.hazard = list(model = "rw1",  scale.model=T))

Firstly I fit the first experiment (2022_04_res_exp1.png) where non of the groups are significant. Here CS residuals are to low indicating that the  mice die to slowly compared to the estimated cumulative hazard rate. Further there are negative CS residuals. Martingale residuals show a clear downwards trend where early indexes consist of the control group.

Secondly, I look ate the same default model for experiment 2 (2022_04_res_exp2.png). Now the treatment effect is significant but has broad credible intervals eg.: mean = 0.13 [0.05, 0.33]. Again, CS residuals are lower than the estimated cumulative hazard rate. However, martingale residuals show a S-curve where the control group has lower values than the treatment group. Deviance residuals are relatively broad with overlapping boxes however the control group (G01) clearly has lower residuals than the rest.

Finally, I include prior information from experiment 1 into experiment 2 and treatment effect is again significant with broad credible intervals. Now the CS residuals mostly fit however the pattern in martingale residuals and deviance residuals (i.e. control group has lower residuals) that has been present without the priors is more pronounced.

Do you have any suggestions how to remove this pattern in the martingale and deviance residuals and make the credible intervals smaller? I am thankful for every suggestion.

I already tried stratification to include a different baseline hazard between control and treatment and inclusion of time based interactions as done here (https://groups.google.com/g/r-inla-discussion-group/c/pBF-pbqsMe0/m/eYQExSSHAAAJ) but can't find a solution to my problem.

All the best and thank you in advance,

Markus

messages.body_plain:
Thank you for the response, Esmail.

I became interested in how INLA::f function works. I have thought that the code below would result in--

f(timeid, model='iid', group='spaceid', control.group=list(model='besag', graph=graph))

kronecker(I_t, D-W), where I_t is a diagonal matrix with the dimension of the number of unique timeids, D is Diagonal(rowSums(W)), and W is a spatial contiguity matrix. But it seems that it works exactly opposite, such that it would give kronecker(D-W, I_t). Please correct me if I am wrong.

The code I attached in the last thread is with minimal edits (for reproducibility) from the example of Blangiardo and Cameletti (2015)'s book <https://sites.google.com/a/r-inla.org/stbook/>, which is one of the most frequently cited references on spatial and spatio-temporal modeling in R-INLA (657 times cited as of April 4, 2022 in Google Scholar). I think their applications using INLA::f function seem not to have the same number of constraints in spatiotemporal interaction models with the number of constraints you explained. My speculation is still very sketchy because I only checked the number of constraints of models with spatiotemporal interaction terms. If my speculation would be found to be (unfortunately) correct, studies that cited their book, including mine, will be severely impacted.

Put it short, I hope I could get any references for the details of how INLA::f works in the context of multilevel models with spatiotemporal interaction terms.

Thank you.
Best,
Insang

I hope I can understand why Type III interaction takes a longer time than other interactions from your insight.

> >
> > Best,

You can try to switch to random walk of order 2 (model="rw2" in control.hazard) for a more smooth baseline curve.

Best,
Denis Rustand

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Re: Slow model fitting with a Type III spatiotemporal interaction
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Re: Slow model fitting with a Type III spatiotemporal interaction
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
the f-models are built from three parts:
  f(A, ..., group = B, ..., replicate = C)
the individual Q-matrices are Q_A, Q_B, and Q_C, where Q_C is an
identity matrix (i.e. like "iid").

The joint precision is
  Q_C x Q_B x Q_A
and the A-part indices vary fastest in the indexing in the internal
latent variable storage, like this:

> expand.grid(a=1:3,b=1:2,c=1:4)
   a b c
1  1 1 1
2  2 1 1
3  3 1 1
4  1 2 1
5  2 2 1
6  3 2 1
7  1 1 2
8  2 1 2
9  3 1 2
...

(note that kronecker ordering conventions aren't universal, so in some
literature it may be written the other way around, but the indexing
above is what determines the ordering in inla)
Typically, I recommend having the most complicated part of the model
as part "A", use replicate for any "iid" kronecker construction, and
group for models less complex than the main "A" part.

But for these "Type I,II,III,IV interaction" models, it becomes rather
complex to specify the models correctly, due to the constraints, and
Esmail's suggestion to construct the constraints numerically from the
actual precision matrices seems like a sensible suggestion to avoid
accidentally missing a constraint, or constructing the wrong
constraints.
It does look like the Blangiardo and Cameletti example (if you
included all constraints set in the book) partly (or even mostly)
ignores the constraints for these models, as it doesn't use
extraconstr at all.  I would suggest contacting the book authors about
that.
There is an Errata on the book webpage at
https://sites.google.com/a/r-inla.org/stbook/errata but this issue
isn't listed there.

Finn

> > It should not be the case: type 3 is slower than type 4. The speed
> > depends on the number of constraints each type has.  The precision
> > matrix is composed of at least 5 blocks: RW (size n) (of order L and
> > L usually equals to 1 or 2), iid (size n, time), besag (size m), iid
> > (size m, space) and rgeneric (type 1,2,3 or 4: which is the
> > Kronecker product of two of the previous models).
> >
> > The number of constraints in each type:
> > 1. type 1: L + 1
> > 2. type 2: Lm + L + 1
> > 3. type 3: n + L + 1
> > 4. type 4: Lm + n - 1
> >
> > Make sure you use the right model for the interaction model using
> > "generic0", and the right rank for the matrix.
> >
> >  f(id,
> >     model="generic0",
> >     Cmatrix = ,
> >     constr= ,
> >     extraconstr = ,
> >     rankdef= )
> >
> > You need to use "extraconstr" to list the constraints you have in
> > each case, which I didn't see in the code. You can use eigen
> > decomposition to find these constraints. "constr" does only sum to
> > zero constraint. However, it can be implemented in different ways,
> > but this is what do I recommend.
> >
> > Best Regards,
> > Esmail
> >
> >
> >
> >
> > On Friday, 3 December 2021 at 00:00:17 UTC+3 sigma...@gmail.com
> > wrote:
> > >
> > > Dear R-INLA community:
> > >
> > > Hello, I am working on models with spatiotemporal interaction
> > > terms.
> > >
> > > I found that fitting models with a type-III (unstructured temporal
> > > * structured spatial) model took a much longer time than fitting
> > > models with the other three types of spatiotemporal interaction
> > > terms. I guessed this is because the rank is a bit higher ((n-1)T;
> > > following Blangiardo and Cameletti 2015:241) than that of other
> > > counterparts, but this does not hold as the type-I interaction has
> > > the higher rank (nT).
> > >
> > > I think this is counterintuitive as well as against the assumption
> > > suggested in Vincente et al. (2020:1429;
> > > https://doi.org/10.1007/s00477-020-01808-x), quote:
> > >
> > > "Regarding computing times for the models presented in Sect. 2,
> > > models with Type II and Type IV interactions are the slowest
> > > regardless of the fitting technique ... One reason for this may be
> > > that the number of constraints is much higher for Type II and Type
> > > IV than for the Type I and Type III counterparts."
> > >
> > > If I understood correctly, the matrix for Type-III would be more
> > > sparse than that of Type-IV, because Type-III takes a diagonal
> > > matrix for the temporal term. A reproducible example taken from
> > > Chapter 7.1.2 in Blangiardo and Cameletti (2015) (attached)
> > > yielded running time in my laptop as below (*please note that no
> > > 'experimental' feature in the up-to-date version of INLA package
> > > was applied here):
> > >
> > > Type I: 10.1 seconds
> > > Type II: 53.1 seconds
> > > Type III: 327 seconds
> > > Type IV: 63.6 seconds
> > >
> > > I am suffering from this issue right now since I aim to compare
> > > four types of spatiotemporal interactions with much larger data.
> > > The model with Type III interaction term with my data (3108*14)
> > > fits terribly slow and consumes 60+GB of memory from time to time
> > > (even with PARDISO and experimental feature of the testing version
> > > of INLA). I hope I can understand why Type III interaction takes a
> > > longer time than other interactions from your insight.
> > >
> > > Thank you very much.
> > >
> > > Best,
>

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I'm fitting a model like the example below. The idea is to kill the model when it runs too long. In the example 1 second, in practice the time-out is set to a much longer time.

model <- try({
    setTimeLimit(cpu = 1, elapsed = 1)
    inla()
  },  silent = TRUE)

Running the code does yield the error message "reached CPU time limit", however also
*** inla.core.safe:  inla.program has crashed: rerun to get better initial values. try=1/2
*** inla.core.safe:  rerun with improved initial values

The output is an inla object instead of a try-error object. It looks like inla() is restarted when killed. Is this intentional?

Best regards,

Thierry

# reproducible example

library(tidyverse)
library(INLA)
set.seed(20180305)
n_id <- 34
n_day <- 7 * 6
n_prompt <- 5
expand.grid(
  ID = seq_len(n_id),
  Day = seq_len(n_day),
  Prompt = seq_len(n_prompt)
) %>%
  mutate(
    Timestamp = runif(n(), min = 8, max = 21.99999),
    Timestamp2 = round(Timestamp, 2),
    Hour = floor(Timestamp)
  ) -> example
data.frame(
  Timestamp2 = seq(min(example$Timestamp2), max(example$Timestamp2), by = 0.01)
) %>%
  mutate(fixed = cumsum(rnorm(n(), sd = 0.05))) -> effect
re <- rnorm(n_id, sd = 0.5)
example %>%
  inner_join(effect, by = "Timestamp2") %>%
  mutate(
    random = re[ID],
    eta = fixed + random,
    mu = plogis(eta + rnorm(n(), sd = 0.1)),
    Craving = rbinom(n(), size = 1, prob = mu),
    DayTime = Day + Timestamp / 24
  ) -> example
pc.prec <- list(theta = list(prior = "pc.prec", param = c(0.5, 0.01)))
model.rw1 <- inla(
  Craving ~ f(Hour, model = "rw1", hyper = pc.prec) + f(ID, model = "iid"),
  family = "binomial",
  data = example,
  control.compute = list(waic = TRUE)
)
model.rw1$cpu.used

model <- try(
  {
    setTimeLimit(cpu = 1, elapsed = 1)
    inla(
      Craving ~ f(Hour, model = "rw1", hyper = pc.prec) + f(ID, model = "iid"),
      family = "binomial",
      data = example,
      control.compute = list(waic = TRUE)
    )
  },
  silent = TRUE
)

messages.body_plain:
``safe=F'' was the default behaviour before it was added in December'21.
with safe=T, then if the model fails to fit, f.ex, it will try various
tricks to improved the initial values and make it work. previously, this
had to be done manually.

I see the issue with timeout, which should be fixed.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Nadeesha,

The error comes from the fact that the weight for time dependent covariates that you are using comes from the baseline hazard intervals [a,b]. You have to use the middle of the interval for an appropriate weight and in your code you are using the value 'a'. Therefore for the first interval, the log of the weight is then the log of zero (=Inf). I fixed it in the attached code.

Now about the error about the breaks not unique, I think it is because you have very few observations so in some situations the "middle breaks" returned by inla.group can have the same value as minimum or maximum values. I also fixed it in the attached code.

Best,
Denis Rustand
he...@r-inla.org

messages.subject_clean: Simulating linear model with INLA
messages.body_plain:
Dear community,

At this link, https://www.r-inla.org/download-install, I found that when simulating a linear model with INLA, the precision parameter has to be explicitly determined.

```
scale = exp(rnorm(n))
prec = scale*tau
y = rnorm(n, mean = eta, sd = 1/sqrt(prec))
```

Why the need of the exponential after extracting the values from the normal distribution as a "scale" object?

Why precision was calculated as scale = exp(rnorm(n)) and prec = scale*tau.

Why not using prec = rnorm(n = n, mean = tau, sd = 1)? Why is there a "scale" which is the exponential of normal data?
I also asked the question here:
https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/570344/simulating-linear-model-with-inla

Thanks for your help !

Bozo

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am wirtting here because I receive the same error message.

I have data on an abundance index (gaussian distribution) for 93 populations along 29 years. In some of these populations, conservation actions have been carried out ("ConservationYes"), whereas in other populations no conservation actions have been carried out. I want to run a spatio-temporal model where I group the spatial field by years (NGroup, w.group), and I replicate it by whether Conservation Actions were carried out or not (Yes/No, 2 iid replicates per year). I do it this way because I aim to assess whether there are differences on the spatio-temporal trends between populations with and without conservation actions. Am I doing it correctly? (please, see the R-code below). I also attach here a .txt file with the Error message received when running the model with verbose = TRUE.

Thank you for your help
Julia

w <- inla.spde.make.index(
  name    = 'w',
  n.spde  = spde$n.spde,
  n.group = NGroup,
  n.repl= NRepl)

f3 <- y ~ -1 + Intercept + ConservationYes + scale(log(Abundance + 1)) +
          f(w,
            model = spde,
            group = w.group,
            replicate = w.repl,
            control.group = list(model='ar1'))

Model <- inla(f3,
           family = "gaussian",

actions. Am I doing it correctly? (please, see the R-code below). I also

Julia

  name    = 'w',

  n.group = NGroup,
  n.repl= NRepl)

          f(w,
            model = spde,
            group = w.group,
            replicate = w.repl,
            control.group = list(model='ar1'))

           family = "gaussian",
           data = inla.stack.data(StackGaussian),
           control.compute = list(waic = TRUE, dic = TRUE),

messages.body_plain:
Make sure to use a sensible scale for the variables. This is easiest done by using appropriate units. Eg. use a different unit for age depending on the oldest person in data. I'd use days when the oldest person is a newborn, months in case of a toddler, years in case of teenagers, decades in case of an elderly person. Likewise don't use meter to express the distance between cities but rather tens, hundreds or even thousands of kilometers.

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Modelling Multinomial data
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Modelling Multinomial data
messages.body_plain:
Hi to all,

Following the example <https://www.r-inla.org/faq#h.u3cjqz72sb5o> in FAQ section in INLA website and thanks to the the advice of Francesco Serafini and his tutorial <https://github.com/inbo/INLA/blob/master/vignettes/multinomial.pdf>, I could estimate a multinomial model like this one (using the variable names in the INLA website example):

head(data)
     y     idx  x1     x2   x3     jdx1  jdx2  jdx3
1   508     1  28.7  4.74  48.3     1     1     1
2   153     1  28.7  4.74  48.3     2     2     2
3   122     1  28.7  4.74  48.3     3     3     3
4   744     2  38.7  2.57  57.0     1     1     1
5   267     2  38.7  2.57  57.0     2     2     2
6   131     2  38.7  2.57  57.0     3     3     3

formula = y ~ -1 +

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,
I am trying to jointly model 2 outcomes with shared random effects (u,v) and extra random terms for the 2nd outcome (u2+v2)
 Y ~ Poisson(r*pop)
log(r1) = intercept1 + u + v
log(r2) = intercept2 + u + v +u2 +v2

I run the code as follows:

n <- nrow(data)
###Response
Y <- matrix(NA, ncol = 2, nrow = 2 * n)
Y[1:n, 1] <- data$y1
Y[n + 1:n, 2] <- data$y2
###Intercept
Inter <- matrix(NA, nrow = 2 * n, ncol = 2)
Inter[1:n, 1] <- 1
Inter[n + 1:n, 2] <- 1
###offset
OS<- c(log(data$pop1),log(data$pop2))
###shared random terms
ID.shared1=c(data$ID,rep(NA,n))
ID.shared2=c(rep(NA,n),data$ID)
# extra random terms for y2
ID.2=c(rep(NA, n),data$ID)

#Model fit
fit.formula <- Y ~ 0 + Inter + offset(OS) +f(ID.shared1, model = "bym",graph=Wmat)+
  f(ID.shared2,copy = 'ID.shared1', model = "bym",graph=Wmat)+f(ID.2, model = "bym",graph=Wmat)

fit2FL <- inla(fit.formula, family = c("poisson", "poisson"),
                      data = list(Y = Y, Inter = Inter,OS=OS, ID.shared1=ID.shared1,
                                  ID.shared2=ID.shared2,ID.2=ID.2),
                      control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
                      control.compute = list(config=T),
                      control.inla=list(strategy="gaussian"))

I want to get estimates for the random terms so I use "summary.random". Based on the way I defined them, I thought that I will only get estimates for the first n rows of ID.shared1, the last n rows of ID.shared2 and the last n rows of ID.2. The rest elements would be blank. Nevertheless, I get estimates for all 2*n rows of each random term.

Is this something to expect or I made a mistake while defining the model?

Thank very much in advance!

Best regards,
Hanah.

messages.subject: Binary data and Error in seq.default and Hyman splinefun
messages.subject_clean: Binary data and Error in seq.default and Hyman splinefun
messages.body_plain:
Dearest R-INLA support community,

We're encountering a problem that is hard to de-bug. Basically, what we want to do is run a series of INLA models on a set of binary variables and it's failing in unexpected ways.

I've opted for a for-loop over the traits *, running inla() each time. While running through the loop over the traits, the script unmistakably fails some way in the traits it's looping over and spits out:

Error in seq.default(r[[1L]], r[[2L]], length = n) :
  'from' must be a finite number

What mystifies us is that
a) it makes it a fair way into the loop of traits before failing
b) when we run the trait it is currently on in the loop in isolation outside of the loop inla() completes just fine.

This is starting to make us wonder, is it do with memory somehow? What could be going on? Any and all advice is appreciated!

More details
To make it easier for others to observe and recreate the problem I've set up a little GitHub repos with some scripts and example data. The crucial script is this one:

https://github.com/HedvigS/INLA_problem_binary_variables/blob/0c1f9e815564a1ab29e20587551a1926a50742c7/INLA_featurewise.R

The data the analysis is working with is unfortunately not published just yet, so I've recreated the workflow with a very similar albeit smaller dataset (the Sahul-survey of Reesink, Dunn and others). Ironically, as I'm looping through those using the same set-up I actually fails in a different way.

Error in splinefun(xnew, xx, method = "hyman") : zero non-NA

We would be very grateful for any advice or assistance anyone can give us, in particular when it comes to the seq.default error.

I'm sorry that my attempt at a reprex of sorts has failed. I hope that looking at the code might prove insightful nonetheless.

You will need to clone the entire repos to get all the bits and bobs for the example I've set up. Beware, the scripts will be installing some packages when run (INLA and its dependencies, paceman, tidyverse, reshape2, ape, jsonlite, phytools, missForest and fields. Nothing crazy).

The data is a series of linguistic traits (grammatical) of languages. We're running several different models: one that accounts only for a phylogenetic vcv, one for the spatial vcv, one for a discrete way of spatially grouping languages and then combinations of the previous.

As it stands right now, the script gets through a few features and then fails with the consol output about the seq.default-error. Before doing so it does spit out some warnings about negative Hessian values. For now, I'm just concentrating on solving the issue that's failing the entire run, and then we'll turn our attention to other concerns.

I'd be more than happy to outline more details of what's going on, but I'll keep it relatively short and sweet for the introduction I think.

I'm new to INLA and this community, please forgive me if I've done anything wrong.

All the best! Happy Easter!
Hedvig

* Yes I might re-write with apply() or another solution, but for now it's a for-loop to make it conceptually easy to read.

messages.subject: Establishing influence of fixed effects
messages.subject_clean: Establishing influence of fixed effects
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA community,

I want to establish whether the fixed effects in the model are influential, i.e. whether two levels of the categorical predictor do not overlap with each other. I could think of three different ways of going about it, and I wanted to know if one of these is better and should be preferred and if they are conceptually different from each other. Below I am providing the code with the simulated model and three approaches.

#loading libraries and running the model
library(INLA)
library(dplyr)
library(tidiverse)

set.seed(123)
data <- data.frame(y = rnorm(100, 0, 1)) %>%
  mutate(x = case_when(y<quantile(y,0.5)~sample(c("a","b"),n(), replace = TRUE, p=c(0.85, 0.15)),
                       TRUE~sample(c("a","b"), n(), replace = TRUE, p=c(0.15, 0.85))))

m1 <- inla(y ~ -1 + x, data = data,
           control.compute = list(config = TRUE))

#Approach 1: obtaining differences between two levels from additionally computing posteriors.

m1_post_samples <- inla.posterior.sample(100, m1)

contrast <- inla.posterior.sample.eval(function(...)
{c(xa - xb)},
m1_post_samples)

contrast <- contrast %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  t()

difference_post <- c(quantile(contrast, 0.025), quantile(contrast, 0.975))

#Approach 2: computing linear combinations (the difference between two levels) and checking whether it crosses zero

lc <- inla.make.lincomb(xa = 1, xb = -1)
m2 <- inla(y ~ -1 + x, data = data, lincomb = lc)

difference_lc <- c(m2$summary.lincomb.derived$`0.025quant`, m2$summary.lincomb.derived$`0.975quant`)

#the difference does not overlap with zero
difference_lc

#Approach 3. Visually checking whether the quantiles of two levels overlap (without additionally computing contrasts)

effects <- data.frame(matrix(ncol = 2, nrow = 6)) %>%
  mutate(effects = rep(c("a", "b"), each=3),
    value = c(m1$summary.fixed[1,]$`0.025quant`,
                   m1$summary.fixed[1,]$`0.5quant`,
                   m1$summary.fixed[1,]$`0.975quant`,
                   m1$summary.fixed[2,]$`0.025quant`,
                   m1$summary.fixed[2,]$`0.5quant`,
                   m1$summary.fixed[2,]$`0.975quant`))

ggplot(effects,
       aes(x = value,
           y = effects,
           colour = effects)) +
  geom_point(position = position_dodge(w = 0.9), size = 1)

Thank you very much in advance.

Best,
Alyona

messages.body_plain:
its a little hard without the actual code, but I noted you do not have
an intercept term, so if all covariates are zero, then the probabilties
are all equal. this is what you want ?

intercept=rep(1:3, n)

here I set the intercept to sum to zero, but you can also fix one of
them to zero without the constraint (although its not *strictly*
correct)

formula = y ~ -1 +  f(intercept, initial=-10,fixed=T,constr=T) +

f(idx, initial = -10, fixed = T) +
f(jdx1, x1, fixed = T, constr = T) +
f(jdx2 x2, fixed = T, constr = T) +
f(jdx3, x3, fixed = T, constr = T) + ...

Hi, thank you for the answer.
Scaling the covariates does not change the situation.

For example, in the following table I'm showing the coefficients of the
complete model (8 covariates):

category 2 as "y" and category 1 as reference.
B1: estimated coefficients of the Poisson model for category 1.

ft         0.18417 694.29214 157.51790 109.32593  0.22688

In the Poisson model, the intercept is a random variable, so I'm showing
the one for the firts observation. I'm also showing the fitted values
(ft), calculated "manually", for this firts observation.

Using the Binomial model, the probability for the first observation is
0.18. Using the Poisson model, the expected value for the condition 2 is
157.52 and the real sample size is 783, so the proportion is 0.2 . The
expected value for category 3 is also accurate, but is not the case for
category 1, however, the predicted value acoording to the model is
516.47, which meets with the restriction, so I suppose that a correction
is applied after. Then I have the probability according to B2-B1 wich is
not bad either (0.23). Actually, this is a spatial model, and the
resulting spatial patterns looks very similar, no matter what model I
use. My problem is when I tried to explain each effect. For example, the
number 7 is negative for B2.B1 (which has not sense at all) but positive
for Bb. The thing is that I'm getting very similar results (fitted
values) with both methods, but with very differents coefficients and
intercepts. Clearly, a magnitude difference has a lot of sense (logits
vs logs, counts vs propabilities), but how a difference in sign can be
explained? Is there a way to fix this? Or simply  the coefficients can't
be interpretated properly if you use the Multinomial-Poisson
transformation?

messages.subject: Posterior Marginals of Intercept
messages.subject_clean: Posterior Marginals of Intercept
messages.body_plain:
Hello!

I am observing peculiar outputs for the posterior marginals of the intercepts (plots attached) from a hurdle model on the joint distribution of occurrence and abundance of invasive plant ("EFB" in code) as a response to various predictors and a shared spatial random effects term. Here's is my current code:

#Response
z <- as.numeric(efb_data$hyd_bin) # EFB occurence, zero-inflated binomial
y <- ifelse(efb_data$EFB_cover > 0, yes=efb_data$EFB_cover,no = NA) #EFB abundance, % cover, beta distribution

##Data Stack
stack.EFB_y <- inla.stack(data = list(alldata = cbind(y,NA)),
                          A = list(A_matrix, 1),
                          effects = list(s.index_mY = spde$n.spde,
                                           list(b0Y = rep(1, nrow(efb_data)),
                                              data.frame(depth=scale(efb_data$wtr_dp_[,1]),
                                              data.frame(typha=scale(efb_data$typ_cover)[,1]),
                                              data.frame(boats=scale(efb_data$NEAR_DIST)[,1]),                                                                    data.frame(fetch=scale(efb_data$MeanFetch)[,1]),
                                              idY = rep(1,nrow(efb_data)), idY2 = rep(1,nrow(efb_data)),                                                        idY3 = rep(1,nrow(efb_data)),
                                              idY4 = rep(1,nrow(efb_data)))),
                          tag = "Beta (EFB Cover)")

#stack for Bernoulli process (EFB occurence)
stack.EFB_z <- inla.stack(data = list(alldata = cbind(NA,z)),
                          A = list(A_matrix, 1),
                          effects = list(s.index_mZ = spde$n.spde,
                                           list(b0Z = rep(1, nrow(efb_data)),
                                              data.frame(depth=scale(efb_data$wtr_dp_[,1]),
                                              data.frame(typha=scale(efb_data$typ_cover)[,1]),
                                              data.frame(boats=scale(efb_data$NEAR_DIST)[,1]),                                                                    data.frame(fetch=scale(efb_data$MeanFetch)[,1]),
                                              idZ = rep(1,nrow(efb_data)), idZ2 = rep(1,nrow(efb_data)),                                                        idZ3 = rep(1,nrow(efb_data)),
                                              idZ4 = rep(1,nrow(efb_data)))),
                          tag = "Bernoulli (EFB Occurence)")

stackm <- inla.stack(stack.EFB_y,stack.EFB_z)

#formula and model run
formula_all <- alldata ~ 0 + b0Y + b0Z +
  f(idY, depth, hyper = FALSE) +
  f(idZ, depth, hyper = FALSE) +
  f(idY2, typha, hyper = FALSE) +
  f(idZ2, typha, hyper = FALSE) +
  f(idY3, boats, hyper = FALSE) +
  f(idZ3, boats, hyper = FALSE) +
  f(idY4, fetch, hyper = FALSE) +
  f(idZ4, fetch, hyper = FALSE)

EFB.hurdlemodel.inla <- inla(formula_all,
                              data = inla.stack.data(stackm),
                              control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stackm),
                                                                link = c(rep(1,length(y)), rep(2,length(z))),                                                                                      compute = TRUE),
                              control.compute = list(dic = T, waic = T, config = T,
                                                                 hyperpar = T, return.marginals=T),
                             family = c("beta", "zeroinflatedbinomial0"),
                             control.family = list(list(link = 'logit'), list(link = 'logit')), verbose = T)

save(EFB.hurdlemodel.inla., file="HurdleModelComplete.RData")

plot(inla.tmarginal(function(x) x, EFB.hurdlemodel.inla$marginals.fixed$b0Y), type ='l')
plot(inla.tmarginal(function(x) x, EFB.hurdlemodel.inla$marginals.fixed$b0Z), type ='l')

Thanks in advance! -Louis J

the 'copy' will copy the whole model , hence you'll get estimate of all
of them even if they are not observed.

Håvard Rue
he...@r-inla.org

-----Original Message-----
From: Hanah <hnhn0...@gmail.com>
To: R-inla discussion group <r-inla-disc...@googlegroups.com>
Subject: [r-inla] Shared random effects - estimates
Date: Thu, 14 Apr 2022 05:14:30 -0700 (PDT)

Hi everyone, I am trying to jointly model 2 outcomes with shared random effects (u,v)
and extra random terms for the 2nd outcome (u2+v2)
 Y ~ Poisson(r*pop)
log(r1) = intercept1 + u + v
log(r2) = intercept2 + u + v +u2 +v2

I run the code as follows:

n <- nrow(data)
###Response
Y <- matrix(NA, ncol = 2, nrow = 2 * n)
Y[1:n, 1] <- data$y1
Y[n + 1:n, 2] <- data$y2
###Intercept
Inter <- matrix(NA, nrow = 2 * n, ncol = 2)
Inter[1:n, 1] <- 1
Inter[n + 1:n, 2] <- 1
###offset
OS<- c(log(data$pop1),log(data$pop2))
###shared random terms
ID.shared1=c(data$ID,rep(NA,n))
ID.shared2=c(rep(NA,n),data$ID)
# extra random terms for y2
ID.2=c(rep(NA, n),data$ID)

#Model fit
fit.formula <- Y ~ 0 + Inter + offset(OS) +f(ID.shared1, model =
"bym",graph=Wmat)+

model = "bym",graph=Wmat)

messages.subject: design and standard errors
messages.subject_clean: design and standard errors
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,
I was thinking about using INLA results from a spatial model for the purposes of design selection (e.g. for selecting additional observation points in order to minimize maximal sd  for fitted.values on a prespecified grid, and similar criteria).

My problem is that the details of the sd field over the grid are influenced by the mesh - leading to kind of granular detailed structure.

Example of this granular structure can be seen on the bottom right picture of Fig 2.10 in chapter 2.5.3 of Advanced Spatial Modeling with Stochastic Partial Differential Equations Using R and INLA.

Even more extreme example is on the attached picture that shows sd's for fitted.values from one of my models. Dots are showing the mesh points. So, it seems that we get higher sd's at mesh points (then bit lower along the edges) and lower values inbetween. I guess that this arises due to interpolation on which 2 (along the edge) or 3 (within triangles) mesh point values participate and lead to higher precision. This seems a bit artificial for the design purposes.

Would it be reasonable to take the sd^2 values at the mesh points and interpolate them, instead? If yes, what interpolation would you recommend? If not, would you recommend to do something else?

All the Best
 Marek

We are using R-INLA within a Bayesian Hierarchical Model (BHM) to solve the sea level budget at a global scale, which involves multiple satellite and in-situ observations and a number of latent processes (roughly 5-7 depending on the set up). This is part of a 6 year project called GlobalMass (www.globalmass.eu <http://www.globalmass.eu>) that is nearing its end. The person who developed the BHM has left the project and we urgently need some support from someone with experience using R-INLA for environmental science (i.e. spatio-temporal) problems. We can offer up to 1.0 FTE until August 2023 for this support so if you are at the end of a contract or have some spare capacity to work on an exciting but challenging problem please get in touch. The team is based at University of Bristol but remote working is possible of course and the PI is also based at Technical University Munich.

Jonathan Bamber (j.ba...@bristol.ac.uk or j.ba...@tum.de)

messages.subject_clean: Interpreting CPO Scores
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have some trouble understanding CPO scores,

CPO_i = p(y_i | y_(-i) ) ,

and how they can be interpreted to identify surprising observations.

It seems to me the CPO is highly dependent on the variability of y | y_(-i). For instance, if

y | y_(-1) ~ N(0, 1)
and
y | y_(-2) ~ N(0, 10^6)

CPO_2 will likely be MUCH smaller than CPO_1, even if y_1 and y_2 are both plausible values given their respective distributions.

In "Implementing Approximate Bayesian Inference using Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation: a manual for the inla program", page 59, it is mentioned that the CPOs must be calibrated, and one way to do this is through PITs. Are the PITs the calibrated values themselves, or a means to calibrate the CPO scores?

Thanks,
Paul

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Interpreting CPO Scores
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Interpreting CPO Scores
messages.body_plain:
Hi Paul,

The behaviour of log p(y_i|y_{-i}) is probably best understood through the lens of proper scoring rules (see e.g. Gneiting and Raftery’s JASA paper from 2005 or 2007),
As it’s essentially the log-score.

When the true predictive distribution is G, and the claimed predictive distribution is F, and the observed value is y, let the score be S(F,y). (For cpo, the distributions are the leave-one-out predictive distributions) log-cpo is a positively oriented score, I.e. a large value is “good”.
A proper score has the property that the expectation over the true distribution is optimized when the claimed distribution F matches the true one, G, I.e.
  S(F,G) := E_{y~G}[S(F,y)]
Is maximized when F=G.

Assume that the true predictive distribution is G~N(0,1). Then F~N(0,10^6) and F~N(0,10^{-6}) would received a lower score than F~N(0,1), on average.
So we can use proper scores to compare different predictions under the same circumstances, e.g. two different models for the same data.

But in your example it seems you wanted to change what you were conditioning _on_, but that’s not the situation handled by these methods. They only cover the case when there is a fixed (but unknown) distribution to be predicted.

So the total sum or average of log-cpo values isn’t really useful in itself. But if you take the pairwise differences between the scores computed from two different models for the same data, then they become more comparable. The variability of each difference still depends on the true G_i distribution, but at least the ordering is informative.
If one knew the true G_i, one could compute the theoretical maximum score expectation, but that’s only possible in toy examples where the true conditional distributions is already known (and these aren’t always philosophically well-defined).

For internal model validation, the pit values are much more meaningful, as they are interpretable for a single model, without the need to compare with another model.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
The old code likely needs to be updated, but we're in the process of
implementing sf support since rgdal etc are being retired soon. In the
meantime, the fm_* functions in inlabru may have more bug fixes than
the sp-functions in INLA; eventually all of these will be in the new
fmesher package instead to make it easier to maintain a coherent
codebase. We've started an sf-support branch for inlabru that has an
experimental mesh-to-sf converter.
Whether that's useful depends on what problem you're trying to solve.
Finn

Hi everyone,

I am modelling fish biomass across the North Sea using a spatio-temporal tweedie georeferenced point model. I've made some very crude pictures to try and explain, in case anyone can offer some advice (code and data also attached in reply thread).

They're are regions (circled red above) that have high biomass, but these regions are predicted low biomass by the model when fitted with a fine scale prediction stack. These regions also have a high spatial correlation that has been removed by the spde random effect (also circled red, below).

I think the spde spatial effect is removing the effect of these high biomass regions and they are not being predicted by the model, can anyone offer some advice?

Sylvan

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Spatial Random Effect taking too much variation in model
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Spatial Random Effect taking too much variation in model
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
The spde field doesn’t “remove correlation”. It captures aspects of spatial variation not captured by other components. So it seems to me what you’re showing is that if you don’t include the spde estimate in your spatial prediction, you’re missing out on biomass that isn’t explained by the rest of the model. Then, in order to produce sensible spatial predictions, you must include the spde part of the model in the spatial predictions.

But perhaps I’m misunderstanding what you’re including in your prediction expression?

(Also note that for complex observation models where predictions are needed on the observation level, not just the parameter level, one needs use posterior sampling to include the variability of the observation level as well.)

Finn

messages.body_plain:
I can’t look at the zip file until later, but the keys are likely a) what components you’re including in the prediction, and b) whether it’s spatio-temporal infill prediction or prediction into the future.

Since you showed fine scale spde field predictions that included the high values at the mentioned locations, presumably you did not include the spde component in your biomass predictions, as then it should have included those hotspot effects; it’s not clear if you included the spde component in your biomass predictions or not. If you didn’t, that’s why it underpredicts at those locations. If you did include it, then that’s a different story.

“The model” consists of the combination of _all_ your model components, so a prediction that doesn’t include the spde component shouldn’t expect to capture phenomena that the spde component was needed for.

Finn

messages.subject: Modelling quadratic relationships using a squared copy of random effects
messages.subject_clean: Modelling quadratic relationships using a squared copy of random effects
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am wondering if it is possible to squared a copy of a random effect.

I am working on a joint spatial model to deal with spatial misalignment. I want to model a quadratic relationship between a Poisson response variable Y (species abundance) and a Normal covariate X (like temperature) that are spatially misaligned, Y and X have been sampled at different locations.
Thus, I use a spatial joint model that first predict covariate values at response locations, and then use those predicted values (pred.X) to estimate coefficient parameters describing the relationship between X and Y.
For a linear relationship between predicted X and Y (Y ~ b0 + b1 * pred.X) the code for the formula used in inla() looks like this:

    formula <- y ~ -1 +
      f(X.field, model = spde) +
      intercept +
      f(predX.field,
        copy = "X.field",
        fixed = FALSE,
        hyper = list(prec = list(param = prior.b)))

Is it possible to extend this for a quadratic relationship between predicted X and observed Y (Y ~ b0 + b1 * pred.X + b2 * (pred.X^2))? Something that could look like:

    formula <- y ~ -1 +
      f(X.field, model = spde) +
      intercept +
      f(predX.field,
        copy = "X.field",
        fixed = FALSE,
        hyper = list(prec = list(param = prior.b))) +
      f(I(predX.field ^ 2),
        copy = "X.field",
        fixed = FALSE,
        hyper = list(prec = list(param = prior.b)))

Any ideas will be appreciated.

Thank you for your time.
Bastien

messages.body_plain:
Hi Richard,

I just stumbled across your post from last year while searching for something else, and read the thread with interest. In particular since I am a coauthor of "phyr", and coded up the INLA based portion of the package, and I'm always looking to improve it. I was unaware of the "generic2" formulation of the model (phyr uses "generic0"). Reading the paper linked to in animalINLA, my interpretation is that the "generic2" and "generic0" setup are equivalent accept that the "generic2" makes it easier to estimate the derived h^2 heritability parameter (which is rarely used in phylogenetic analyses in my experience). The paper also claims "generic2" setup does not give correct DIC measures but "generic0" does. Since model comparison is of interest in phyr, so far I am leaning towards keeping that formulation. In your experience have you found any other benefits of using "generic2"? I don't know if the same issue applies to WAIC though, which I prefer to use over DIC anyway. Anyone here know about this?

I wanted to ask what you meant by the scaling used in the phyr example leading to "incorrect" estimates? Incorrect estimates of the fixed effects? Note that the scaling done by MCMCglmm:inverseA simply scales the phylogeny to have a root to tip distance of 1, before doing the inversion (and only works on an ultrametric tree). The scaling in the phyr example (Vphy <- Vphy/(det(Vphy)^(1/nspp))) is instead scaling the covariance matrix itself in order to have a generalised variance of 1. This is to make results of the model more comparable across models, even ones using different phylogenies. This rescaling however changes the scale of the precision matrix such that the prior might have to be reformulated with this taken into account, which is possibly why you got different estimates than you were expecting.

Note that phyr also uses MCMCglmm::inverseA internally to calculate the correct precision matrix, however, at the moment we use the tips-only option. I also came to the conclusion some time ago that we should use the whole phylogeny, including internal nodes to calculate the precision matrix, and include missing data for the internal nodes. This as mentioned above should be more accurate but I have also found for large phylogenies it is orders of magnitude faster, presumably because the full precision matrix is sparse, whereas the tips-only covariance matrix is dense, and INLA is very efficient for sparse matrices (this still seems very counter-intuitive to me, but I have been convinced by experience that it is true). Anyway, I have not yet had the time to implement this change in phyr yet partly because the main effects of interest in phyr are the 'nested' phylogenetic effects, which actually use the Kronecker product of the phylogenetic covariance and an iid covariance for the "sites", and I need to think carefully about how to do this correctly with the internal nodes (it is probably not as complicated as I think). I have been wondering for awhile whether I could use the "group" argument of f() to accomplish an equivalent model, but haven't had time to look into it properly. If anyone has any thought on this, I would love to hear them!

All the best,
Russell
--
Russell Dinnage PhD
Research Assistant Professor
Institute of Environment
Department of Biological Sciences
Florida International University
Miami, Florida, United States

The latter solved the problem of intercept posteriors being too tight and non-overlapping with the true value.
>

Just as a side note, the function MCMCglmm::inverseA correctly scales the inverse covariance matrix for the phylogeny (by default). I'm not sure if this is true for the package 'phyr' - I followed the instructions in the example under ?pglmm and got a differently scaled matrix that produced incorrect estimates in the analysis.
>
> > Does this mean you have only a single record per each level of spN?
>
> In these simulated datasets, yes (and that's pretty common in phylogenetic comparative analyses). In the MCMCglmm model, the residual variance is the variance in y left unexplained by the phylogenetic covariance matrix (the random effect), which assumes Brownian motion evolution.
>

I hope this makes sense. Say you have 5x5 precision matrix, so 1:N is 1:5. Then say that you have observations on 3, 4 and 5 (the tips), then your spN column in the phenotype data will only have 3, 4 and 5. You will then get estimates for all 5 effects, spN1, spN2, spN3, spN4 and spN5 - since they are all connected via the precision matrix.
> >
> > Are you fitting the same model in MCMCglmm? I am not fully clear, but from your description it seems you are thinking about phenotype = 1 Interecept + u (so not Zu, and also no residual). Does this mean you have only a single record per each level of spN? If so, then indeed you won't have sufficient data structure to separate u and e (the "Zu + e" is just "u + e"). You can use control.family to fix sigma2e to a "numerical" zero then, but be careful that the theta in control.family is (see documentation).

As a side note, in the ?MCMCglmm documentation under the option 'nodes' it says: "...For phylogenies "TIPS" estimates effects for the tips only, and for pedigrees a vector of ids can be passed to nodes specifying the subset of individuals for which animal effects are estimated. Note that all analyses are equivalent if omitted nodes have missing data but by absorbing these nodes the chain max mix better. I think the INLA model may be interpreting the phylogenetic random effect as an additional 'phylogenetic noise' component on top of the linear fixed-effect model, rather than treating it as statistical non-independence. So fitting a model like:
> > >

Furthermore, you could be interested in the inferred value of "internal" nodes in your downstream analysis (after model fitting). Also, subsetting covariance matrix and inverting it is in essence still estimating all the nodes, but not directly - the removed nodes become part of your model with more involved precision matrix between the sample nodes (tips) - precision matrix of the subset will be denser and indicate the relationships between your samples nodes (tips) due to removed internal nodes.

> > > > > > > I'm currently trying to replicate the following MCMCglmm model using INLA, but without success so far. The objective is to estimate the coefficients of effects of 'fixed effect' predictors on the response while controlling for non-independence among data points (species) due to their evolutionary relationships ('phylogeny'). According to a Brownian motion model, which I'm assuming, the covariance among data points (species) drops linearly and proportionally with increasing distance in evolutionary time.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > A phylogeny in this case is an ultrametric bifurcating representation of evolutionary distances in time ('branch lengths') among species, with tips (the individual species) connected by internal nodes (which also connect to each other via other nodes), and a root node connecting everything. > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > #############################################
> > > > > > > #Example MCMCglmm analysis setup on a simulated dataset#

> > > > > > >
